title: Discovery and scoping
summary: How to turn a client's vague app idea into a small, signed, testable MVP before you quote or write a line of code.
youWillLearn: Why you never quote or build straight from a client's first description
How discovery finds the real problem behind a feature wish
How to write user stories with acceptance criteria a client can test
How to cut a wish list down to an MVP and write the scope on one page

glossary.discovery: A short phase before the build where you learn the client's real problem, users and limits, and turn them into a plan.
glossary.MVP: Minimum viable product: the smallest version of the app that solves the core problem well enough to launch to real users.
glossary.user story: A one-line need written from a user's view: as a [who], I want [what], so that [why].
glossary.acceptance criteria: Concrete checks that prove a user story is done. If all pass, the story is finished; if not, it is not.
glossary.MoSCoW: A way to sort features into Must have, Should have, Could have and Won't have (this time).
glossary.scheduler: A timer that runs a piece of the app's code at set times, for example every hour.
glossary.assumption: Something the plan takes as true without proof yet. Writing it down makes the risk visible to both sides.
glossary.scope creep: A project growing slowly through many small additions that nobody estimated or agreed to pay for.
glossary.change request: A written request for work outside the agreed scope, estimated and approved before anyone builds it.
glossary.spike: A short, throwaway experiment to learn how hard an unknown part is before you commit to a price.

steps.title: Meet Sam and her salon
body: Sam owns a small hair salon with four stylists. Her clients book by phone, and she writes every appointment in a paper diary.
Sam wants an app for this, and has asked you to build it: you ship apps with Claude Code. This lesson is your first project with her, from the first call to a signed plan.

callout.text: This module follows Sam's project from start to finish: discovery, price, contract, handoff and support. Each lesson starts from where the last one ended.

scene.caption: Today: clients phone Sam, and she writes each booking in a paper diary.

steps.title: A wish is not a spec
body: On your first call Sam says: "I want an app where clients book, pay and get reminders. Maybe some AI too."
That sentence could be a two-week build or a six-month one. Quote it now and you are guessing. Start building now and you will probably build the wrong half.

callout.text: A client tells an architect: "a house with a nice kitchen". Nobody pours concrete yet. First come questions, then drawings, then a price.

changes: + App Idea: Sam's wish, in one sentence
~ Wish list 0 → 4: book, pay, remind, AI
~ Size guess unknown → 2 weeks to 6 months
~ Salon Clients and Paper Diary fade back

scene.caption: Sam's idea arrives as one vague sentence. Its real size is unknown.

steps.title: Discovery comes before any price
body: Before any estimate comes discovery: one or two sessions where you find the real problem behind the wish.
What comes out is an MVP, a minimum viable product: the smallest version that solves that problem for real users. Not a demo, and not every idea. The first thing worth launching.

callout.text: You already do this as a designer: research, problem framing, prioritizing. Discovery is the same craft, with a technical plan and a price at the end. Many freelancers charge for it as a small first project.

changes: ~ App Idea → Discovery: questions before a price
+ MVP: the smallest version worth launching

scene.caption: Discovery sits between the wish and the build. What comes out is small and clear.

steps.title: Ask about today, not about features
body: Ask what happens today. Sam answers the phone between haircuts, so calls get missed. And about one client in ten forgets their appointment.
Now you have real problems: missed calls and no-shows. Keep asking: who books, how often, what does an empty chair cost, and what would success look like in three months?

callout.text: Write answers as numbers when you can. "About 1 in 10 no-shows" becomes your success measure later: did reminders bring it down?

changes: + No-shows: about 1 client in 10 forgets
~ Salon Clients back: their calls to Sam get missed
~ MVP fades back while you listen

scene.caption: Questions about today reveal two concrete problems behind the wish.

steps.title: User stories make features testable
body: Zoom in. Write each need as a user story: as a [who], I want [what], so that [why]. Missed calls become Book Online, no-shows become Get Reminders, the paper diary becomes Owner Calendar.
Add acceptance criteria: checks that prove it is done. "Reminders work" is a feeling. "A text 24 hours before each booking" is a test.

code.code:
Story: As a client, I want to book online,
  so that I don't have to call during work hours.

Acceptance criteria:
- I see free slots for the next 4 weeks
- I pick a service, a stylist, then a slot
- A slot can never be booked twice
- I get an email confirmation within a minute
code.caption: Each criterion is something Sam can check herself on her phone.

changes: − Salon Clients, Sam, Paper Diary, Discovery, MVP, No-shows
+ Book Online, Get Reminders, Owner Calendar: one story per need
+ Checks: four criteria that prove Book Online is done

scene.caption: Three needs become three stories. Each story gets checks that prove it is done.

steps.title: Must, should, could, won't
body: Sam's list keeps growing. Sort it with MoSCoW: must have for launch, should have soon, could have someday, won't have this time. Online payment is a Should. The MVP is the Must column only.
Writing down the Won't column matters as much. It is the line you point to when someone says "I thought that was included".

callout.text: Packing a carry-on. Everything you want is on the bed. Only what fits goes in the bag, and you decide that at home, not at the gate.

changes: − Checks
+ Must have: the three stories, now the MVP
+ Won't have: AI Rebooking, Loyalty Points, Native App
~ Wish list 4 → 7, In the MVP 0 → 3, Size guess → 3–4 weeks

scene.caption: Three stories make the MVP. Three ideas wait, written down, for later.

steps.title: Sketch the parts behind the stories
body: Each Must story needs parts. Clients book in a browser on their phone. The app server, the computer running the salon's code, saves each booking in a database (its storage).
Reminders hide more: a scheduler wakes the app server every hour, and an SMS service, an outside company, sends the texts. One word on the list, two extra parts.

code.caption: One row per booking. reminder_sent_at stays empty until the text goes out, so nobody gets it twice.
code.code:
create table bookings (
  id uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  client_id uuid not null references clients(id),
  stylist_id uuid not null references stylists(id),
  starts_at timestamptz not null,
  reminder_sent_at timestamptz
);
code.caption: A first sketch, not the final design. It is enough to see the work and spot the unknowns.

changes: − Book Online, Get Reminders, Owner Calendar
− AI Rebooking, Loyalty Points, Native App
+ Browser, App Server, Database: the booking site
+ Scheduler, SMS Service: the parts behind reminders

scene.caption: The Must stories drawn as parts. Reminders alone need three of them.

steps.title: One page that Sam signs
body: Wrap discovery in one page: the problem, a success measure, the Must stories with criteria, the Won't list, and each assumption.
Assumptions are bets you say out loud: one location, English only, Sam supplies prices and photos. If one turns out false, the scope changes, and you both saw it coming.

code.code:
Problem:  missed calls, ~1 in 10 no-shows
Success:  bookings online, fewer no-shows in 3 months

Must:     online booking, SMS reminders, owner calendar
Should:   online payment, right after launch
Won't v1: AI rebooking, loyalty points, native app

Assumptions:
- One location, 4 stylists, English only
- Sam supplies services, prices and photos
- The salon pays SMS costs directly

callout.text: Claude Code can turn your call notes into stories and a scope doc in minutes. Then check: did it add features nobody asked for? Ask it to list assumptions and open questions separately. Can a non-developer test every criterion?

changes: − Browser, App Server, Database, Scheduler, SMS Service
+ Scope Doc: one page with Musts, Won'ts and assumptions
+ You write it, Sam signs it

scene.caption: Discovery ends with one signed page that both sides can point to.

steps.title: Scope creep and the vague AI feature
body: Scope creep rarely arrives as one big ask. It comes as ten small ones: "could it also…". Each sounds reasonable. Together they double the project.
AI features creep fastest: "add some AI" has no finish line. Pin it down: what goes in, what comes out, three examples of a good answer. New ideas go through a change request.

callout.text: Never meet a risky integration for the first time after you quote. If the SMS service or a calendar sync is unknown, run a short spike during discovery: a throwaway test to learn how hard it really is.

changes: + Small Asks: "could it also…", one at a time
+ Change Request: each new ask written and priced
~ Scope Doc under pressure
~ Wish list 7 → 10

scene.caption: Small asks pile onto the signed scope. A change request prices each one first.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: A wish is not a spec. Discovery finds the real problem and shrinks it to an MVP: Must stories with acceptance criteria, a written Won't list and stated assumptions, on one page Sam signs.
Everything new after that is a change request with its own price. Estimating that price is the next lesson.
changes: − The dashed shortcut from Small Asks into the Scope Doc
+ Change Request → Scope Doc: approved asks join it
~ Scope Doc: signed and steady

scene.caption: New asks reach the scope only through a priced change request.

quiz.question: On the first call Sam says: "Build me an app like the big booking platforms. How much?" What is the best next move?

options.text: Give a ballpark now so she does not lose interest.
options.why: A number said out loud sticks. With no scope behind it, it is either too low (you lose money) or too high (you lose the deal).

options.text: Propose a short discovery phase, then a written estimate.
options.why: Discovery turns "like the big platforms" into a small, specific MVP. Then the estimate has something real to rest on.

options.text: Start a prototype with Claude Code tonight to impress her.
options.why: Fast building of the wrong thing is still the wrong thing. You do not know yet which problem she most needs solved.

quiz.question: Which of these is a usable acceptance criterion for "clients get reminders"?

options.why: "Reliably" cannot be tested. You and Sam could each read it differently.

options.text: Reminders use a modern SMS service.
options.why: That describes how it is built, not what the client experiences. It does not prove the story is done.

options.text: Each client with a booking gets a text 24 hours before it.
options.why: It is concrete and checkable: make a booking, wait, see if the text arrives at the right time.

quiz.question: Halfway through the build, Sam asks: "Could the app also suggest the best time to rebook, with AI?" What do you do?

options.text: Write it up as a change request: inputs, outputs, examples, estimate.
options.why: It is on the signed Won't list. A change request makes the new work visible and priced before anyone builds it.

options.text: Add it quietly; it is only one AI call.
options.why: The AI call is the easy part. Prompting, edge cases, testing and running costs add up, and you are now working unpaid.
The scope protects both sides; it is not a wall. Good ideas are welcome through the change process.

takeaways: Never quote or build from the first description. Run discovery first, ideally as a small paid step.
Ask about what happens today and capture numbers. They become your success measure.
Write user stories with acceptance criteria a non-developer can test.
The MVP is the Must column. Write the Won't list and your assumptions down too.
Anything new after sign-off is a change request: written, estimated, approved.
